extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy, constitutional designers, and informed citizens
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and evaluates normative criteria for constitutional design and forms of government (checks and balances, accountability, representation, protection of property and liberty) as argued from historical examples. Intended to guide judgment about which government structures preserve liberty and property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard constitution against tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: The constitution should be guarded at all points against tyranny; against the tyranny of the one, the few, and the many.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author insists lawgivers and philosophers should enlighten the people's understandings and erect safeguards so that killing a tyrant does not simply make way for a worse one; constitutional provisions must prevent concentration or abuse of power in any form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educate the citizenry about government and liberties
rubrics_metrics.description: Enlighten the people's understandings, and improve their morals, by good and general education; enable them to comprehend the scheme of government and to know upon what points their liberties depend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education is necessary to dissipate vulgar prejudices and superstitions that oppose good government and to teach that obedience to laws is as indispensable in citizens as in lords and kings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability of officers and governors
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom is to be preserved no other way in a commonwealth, but by keeping officers and governors in an accountable state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officers must be questionable and callable to account (e.g., by assemblies) so that standing powers do not become unaccountable; the English constitution is praised for enabling officers to be called to account without extreme difficulty or widespread bloodshed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of powers (three branches reciprocally dependent)
rubrics_metrics.description: A government of three branches, reciprocally dependent on each other, brings men to taste of subjection as well as rule and prevents arbitrary power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text cites triadic separation of functions (legislative, executive, judicial) as the only reliable safeguard against tyranny and as enabling effective accountability without assassination or bloodshed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid concentration of authority in a single sovereign assembly
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons in power cannot be brought to account, unless by assassination, in a government by a single sovereign assembly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues historical experience shows single supreme assemblies make peaceful accountability effectively impossible and invite danger and disorder when attempting to check those in power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative bodies must be genuinely representative in composition and selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Assemblies composed of representatives not chosen by the people (appointed by aristocratic regencies, hereditary families, or municipal oligarchies) do not truly represent the people's interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (Swiss cantons, French états-généraux, Aragon) are used to show that how representatives are selected (popular election vs. aristocratic appointment) crucially affects whether assemblies protect property and liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent continuance of power in particular hands (limit re-election/tenure)
rubrics_metrics.description: The government should be so constituted that people cannot permit the continuance of power in particular hands; continuance of power enables creation of parties and popular tumults and leads to abuses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent re-elections or unchecked continuance enable favorites to accumulate power, create parties, inveigle the people, and ultimately turn popular favor into durable domination; constitutional design should limit this tendency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect minority rights against majority tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever placeth every man's right under the will of another is no less than tyranny; the majority can, by common consent (i.e., majority vote), destroy minority rights and property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because unanimity is impossible and 'common consent' practically means majority rule, constitutions must include safeguards preventing the majority from arbitrarily destroying the rights or property of minorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance popular influence in executive and legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever the people have had any share in the executive, or more than one third part of the legislative, they have always abused it and rendered property insecure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that too large a share of executive or legislative power vested in popular bodies tends to instability and insecurity of property; therefore, limits on popular control of executive or legislative composition are advised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent judiciary as a check on executive power
rubrics_metrics.description: A judicial officer (e.g., a chief justice) empowered to control the king if he acted illegally and accountable to representative bodies is a powerful check.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (Arragon) show that having an independent judicial authority that can controul the executive and is publicly accountable helps preserve laws and resist arbitrary royal acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent ruling party's appropriation of public funds and offices
rubrics_metrics.description: If the ruling party can dispose of all offices, annex salaries and fees, lay taxes, appropriate public money, and decide causes by their own judgments, property and liberty become insecure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fiscal and administrative controls (transparent appropriation, neutral administration, legal limits) are necessary to stop parties from enriching themselves and impoverishing opponents through state mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design constitutions with realistic view of human passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws of nature or moral codes are insufficient because human passions will violate them; therefore constitutions must restrain passions by institutional design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The argument stresses that because men will swerve from rules under passion, institutions must be constructed so that individuals cannot easily violate fundamental laws — structural restraints are required, not mere moral exhortation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that historical forms can degenerate into demagoguery or standing power
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical cases (Athens, Sparta, Rome) show that assemblies or standing magistrates, once unbalanced or captured by powerful men, lead to parties, tumults, and ultimately loss of liberty and property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical exemplars as cautionary evidence: institutions that look free can be subverted by leaders (Pericles, Caesar, Marius, Sylla) who exploit assemblies or popular favour to concentrate power; thus anticipate and guard against such degeneration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unanimity impractical — build checks because majority rule needs protection
rubrics_metrics.description: If 'common consent' were unanimous it might protect rights, but unanimity is impossible; therefore, majority rule requires institutional constraints to prevent its tyranny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional design should assume majority decisions will prevail and thus embed safeguards (separation of powers, bicameralism, judicial review, term limits) to mitigate majoritarian abuses.
